summary: Registers header fields for Internet mail that carry the service elements of a Military Message Handling System, which is defined in X.400-based standards such as STANAG 4406 and ACP 123. It also covers a gateway between STANAG 4406 and Internet email. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Armed forces have their own messaging system with special labels. This defines matching labels for ordinary email, so messages can cross between the two worlds.

questions: military message handling in internet email
how to send military emails through internet
subtitle: Header fields for military message services in Internet email.

tldr.problem: Military message handling systems (X.400-based STANAG 4406 and ACP 123) define special service elements that do not map directly to Internet email, making it difficult to gateway messages between military and standard email networks.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6477 registers 14 new MMHS-prefixed header fields for Internet email that carry military messaging service features like precedence levels, message types, distribution codes and handling instructions.
tldr.outcome: Messages can now be converted between military and standard email systems while preserving service information, supporting interoperability between NATO and national military messaging systems and public Internet mail.

today: RFC 6477 remains an active informational specification. It defines the Internet mail equivalent of the military messaging standards STANAG 4406 and ACP 123, enabling gateways between military and civilian email systems. The specification is maintained by the IESG on behalf of the IETF and the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) maintains the registry of MMHS header fields.

sections.title: Military Messages and Internet Email
sections.content:
RFC 6477 defines a set of new email header fields that enable military messaging to work with Internet mail. Military Message Handling System (MMHS) is the standard for international military communications, defined in STANAG 4406 Edition 2 and ACP 123. These military standards are based on X.400, the international email standard from the 1990s.

The problem is that MMHS defines messaging services and features that Internet email (RFC 5322) does not have. When military and civilian email systems need to exchange messages through a gateway, the service information gets lost. This RFC solves that by creating new header fields that carry the military service elements in a format that Internet email systems understand and can pass through.

All 14 header fields defined here are prefixed with MMHS- to clearly distinguish them from standard Internet email headers. They are all optional in Internet messages, so regular email continues to work unchanged.
sections.eli5: When military people send messages through internet email, they need special labels that internet email did not have before. This creates those labels so the military information does not get lost.

sections.title: The 14 Military Header Fields
sections.content:
RFC 6477 registers the following header fields:

Recipient and addressing fields: MMHS-Exempted-Address lists people in a mailing list who should not receive the message. MMHS-Other-Recipients-Indicator-To and MMHS-Other-Recipients-Indicator-CC name primary and copy recipients who got the message through channels other than MMHS (for instance, via a phone call or a separate network).

Precedence and handling: MMHS-Primary-Precedence and MMHS-Copy-Precedence set the priority level (deferred, routine, priority, immediate, flash, or override, or numeric 0-5) for action and information recipients respectively. MMHS-Handling-Instructions and MMHS-Message-Instructions carry human-readable notes for traffic operators (handling) and message readers (instructions).

Message classification: MMHS-Message-Type marks whether the message is an exercise, operation, project, or drill, optionally with a name. MMHS-Subject-Indicator-Codes carries distribution codes (3 to 8 characters each) used to route the message within receiving organizations.

Authorization and references: MMHS-Extended-Authorisation-Info holds the date and time when the message was released by an authorized officer. MMHS-Originator-Reference is a user-defined reference number assigned by the originating unit.

Legacy and ACP 127 support: MMHS-Codress-Message-Indicator, MMHS-Acp127-Message-Identifier, and MMHS-Originator-PLAD are used only when interfacing with older tape relay systems (ACP 127) or the X.400 Codress format where addresses are encrypted in the message body.
sections.eli5: The 14 fields carry different kinds of military information: who should not get it, how fast it should be handled, what kind of exercise it is, date stamps, reference numbers, and sometimes old-fashioned forms of the address.

sections.title: Field Values and Syntax
sections.content:
Each header field has a formal syntax defined in RFC 5234 (ABNF). Most precedence and message-type fields accept both symbolic names and numeric values. For example, MMHS-Primary-Precedence: FLASH is the same as MMHS-Primary-Precedence: 4. The six standard precedence levels use values 0 to 5, but the spec reserves 0-15 for NATO use and 16-31 for national extensions, allowing countries to define their own priority levels.

Dates in MMHS-Extended-Authorisation-Info follow RFC 5322 format (for example, Mon, 09 Aug 2010 15:27:40 +0100). Military string fields like MMHS-Handling-Instructions can be up to 69 characters and may contain semicolon-separated sequences, and address fields use standard RFC 5322 email address syntax.

No header field may appear more than once in a message. The specification is designed so that these headers can be mechanically converted to and from the corresponding X.400 heading extensions in STANAG 4406.
sections.eli5: Each field has rules about what values it can hold. Some use words (like FLASH), some use numbers (like 4), and some hold email addresses or dates. The syntax ensures that military and internet email systems can translate between each other without mistakes.

sections.title: Gateways Between Military and Internet Mail
sections.content:
A gateway between MMHS (X.400/STANAG 4406) and Internet mail (SMTP/RFC 5322) uses this specification to convert messages bidirectionally. When an X.400 message with MMHS heading extensions arrives at the gateway, the gateway generates the corresponding RFC 6477 header fields in the outgoing Internet message. When an Internet message with these headers enters an X.400 system, the gateway encodes them as X.400 heading extensions.

The conversion is not perfect for a few features that MMHS defines but this RFC does not implement: security information labels (deprecated in favor of S/MIME), address list indication (deprecated), pilot forwarding information, and ACP 127 notification requests and responses. For these unimplemented features, the gateway may discard them or map them in a proprietary way.

When an incoming Internet message contains these MMHS headers, the gateway must encode the outgoing X.400 message as P772 (the MMHS variant). The RFC also specifies detailed rules for handling Message-ID fields to meet ACP 123 constraints (at least 15 characters for the local part) and for gatewaying with the older tape relay system ACP 127.
sections.eli5: A gateway machine sits between military and civilian email systems. When a military message arrives, the gateway translates its special labels into internet email headers. When an internet message arrives, the gateway translates them back. Not every feature translates perfectly, but the most important information gets through.

sections.title: Security and Signature Concerns
sections.content:
RFC 6477 advises that MMHS messages can be protected using S/MIME and DKIM signatures. DKIM is particularly useful because it can protect against alteration or deletion of these header fields, which can affect how the receiving gateway or system processes the message. For example, changing the MMHS-Primary-Precedence field could cause a message to be handled with wrong priority.

A critical security issue arises when messages are gatewayed between MMHS/X.400 and Internet mail: if the original message was digitally signed, converting it breaks the signature because the header fields change. The receiving gateway can sign the translated message itself (using DKIM), but the recipient cannot verify that the message came from the original sender. The RFC notes this limitation and advises that organizations that require end-to-end signatures should consider direct point-to-point connections rather than gateways.
sections.eli5: These headers can be digitally signed to prove nobody changed them. But when a message crosses from military to civilian mail, the signature breaks because the headers change. The new system can sign the message again, but the original sender's signature is lost.
